rv.q: And when the climax you half suspect is coming, comes, it is like a final, epoch ending volcanic eruption, the play's carefully constructed emotional checks and balances detonating in a maelstrom of violence and feeling that left me genuinely stunned.
The Ferryman is profligate, boisterous, far-reaching.
Miss this and you’ve missed a marvel.
This is a richly absorbing and emotionally abundant play, directed with detailed humane mastery by Sam Mendes.
The fiercely gripping play in which Quinn, a father of seven, appears is every bit as crowded.
The acting is pretty spectacular all round.
The Ferryman has lived up to the faith already invested in it.
Jez Butterworth’s vast, sprawling superbly directed (by Sam Mendes) play really does fall into that rare category – unmissable.
The script is deliciously anecdotal, sparkling with humour and it succeeds at painting detailed portraits of well-rounded characters.
With acting like this, it's really an amazing experience, if a rather heartless one. But Butterworth's storytelling finesse carries all before it.

cn.t: Butterworth's epic three-hour family drama set during the Troubles earns near-universal acclaim for its sprawling ambition and gripping storytelling. Critics hail it as a shattering, unmissable theatrical event, though some bristle at the hype.
